Context:
In the mid-1950s, Frank Burnet, inspired by a suggestion made by Niels Jerne, formulated the clonal selection theory (CST) of immunity. On the basis of CST, Burnet developed a theory of how an immune response is triggered according to the self/nonself distinction: "self" constituents (constituents of the body) do not trigger destructive immune responses, while "nonself" entities (pathogens, an allograft) trigger a destructive immune response. The theory was later modified to reflect new discoveries regarding histocompatibility or the complex "two-signal" activation of T cells. The self/nonself theory of immunity and the self/nonself vocabulary have been criticized, but remain very influential.

Question:
What is the complex "two-signal" activation of T cells referred to?

Answer:

response.prediction: The complex "two-signal" activation of T cells refers to the requirement that T cells receive two distinct signals in order to become fully activated and mount an immune response. The first signal is delivered through the T cell receptor (TCR) when it recognizes a specific antigen presented by an antigen-presenting cell (APC) via major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules. The second signal, known as a co-stimulatory signal, is provided by the interaction of co-stimulatory molecules on the APC (such as B7 proteins) with their corresponding receptors on the T cell (such as CD28 on the T cell). This two-signal system ensures that T cells are activated only when they encounter a genuine threat and not in response to self-antigens, thereby helping to prevent autoimmunity.
